old: For that starting point, I use a provisional, author-developed bridge I call borrowed adulthood. It combines familiar practices—witnessing, modeling, supported action, and gradual transfer of responsibility—without claiming that the complete sequence has been validated as one treatment.
new: To jumpstart a development of a new part, I have developed a kind of provisional bridge that I call “borrowed adulthood.” It is important to note here that I’m not suggesting that all of the steps in this process have been formally tested and proven.

old: Witness, when needed. Notice what is present without demanding warmth, wisdom, or certainty. If you already distinguish the internal positions, move to the adult function you need.
new: Access your witnessing position if necessary. If you already know how to access different internal positions, move immediately to accessing the adult position you want to borrow and go to step 3.

old: Borrow one function. Choose a safe adult, mentor, older sibling, future self, spiritual figure, value, or written plan. Borrow only the warmth, boundary, or direction needed now.
new: If you have a safe adult in your life you can borrow from them, if not borrow from a mentor, older brother/sister, imagine your future self, your god/goddess or higher power, a value you have, a plan you have written, etc. It’s ok to just borrow what you need, just like you would borrow a cup of sugar from a neighbor.

old: Become the adult apprentice. Choose the exact words or action yourself and carry at least one small part.
new: Next, put on your adult hat as if you are an apprentice adult and do or say what you think you should do or say. You should do at least part of what you think you should do or say.

old: People assume inner-child work begins with the child. Very often, you meet the guard at the door first.
new: If you're not careful, you might find yourself expecting that when you go within to meet your inner child, you'll find your inner child.

old: You sit down to connect and get numbness, cynicism, anger, sudden hunger, a phone urge, a sexual urge, planning, sleepiness, dissociation, or the thought, “This is stupid.” I wouldn’t call those failures. They’re often the protector making an appearance in its usual charming way.
new: Instead, you might feel numb, cynical, angry, hungry, like you need to look at your phone, sexually aroused, like you need to make plans, sleepy, dissociated, or you might even think that what you're doing is stupid. Those are not failures, they are you experiencing what is often a very charming protector or guard.

old: Rest also doesn’t require helplessness. Reduce decisions for a defined period, put unfinished tasks somewhere visible, and let the internal adult keep watch. You remain able to move, stop, and return.
new: Now, before you get to resting, it’s okay to limit the amount of decisions you are going to be making for a certain amount of time, it’s okay to put the things you might not get to on a list and it’s okay to let your inner adult take over for a while.

old: If the practice makes you more loving, grounded, relational, honest, and functional, continue gently. If it makes you more paranoid, sleepless, grandiose, isolated, frightened, or unreal, stop deepening and get support.
new: One rule of thumb for deciding whether to keep going with something or not in a situation like this is if it’s making you more loving, more grounded, more relational, more honest, more functional, etc, then it’s probably ok to keep doing it, but gently. If it’s making you more Paranoid, more sleepless, more grandiose, more isolated, more scared, more unreal, etc, then don’t go deeper, go and get help.
